title: Alton Locke, Tailor and Poet: An Autobiography
description: Published in 1850 and the first English novel written from inside the Chartist movement: the autobiography of a London tailor-poet who becomes a Chartist orator, is imprisoned, and emigrates to Texas.
plot_or_argument: Alton Locke, a poor tailor's apprentice, educates himself as a poet, is taken up by a wealthy patron and then by the Chartist leader, is involved in the demonstration of 1848, is tried after the riots and dies of consumption on the voyage to America, converted to a Christian socialism by his friend the Scottish bookseller.
principal_characters: Alton Locke; Sandy Mackaye; the Dean; Lady Ellerton; Lillian Winnstay; George Crossthwaite; Alton's mother
historical_context: The 1840s, the sweated tailoring trade, the Chartist petition of 1848, the Kennington Common meeting, and the Christian Socialist movement of Maurice and Ludlow.
literary_significance: Alton Locke is a founding text of the English working-class novel and the most important English fictional record of Chartism: its picture of the sweated tailor's life and of the poetry of a self-taught worker made it a central document of Victorian social history.

title: Yeast: A Problem
description: Published in Fraser's Magazine in 1848 and in book form in 1851: the story of a young aristocrat's education, and the most direct English novel of the religious and social crisis of 1848.
plot_or_argument: Lancelot Smith, a young gentleman, is drawn between the world of the country house and the world of the farm labourer, and between the agonies of doubt and the claims of faith; his friendship with the gamekeeper's family and his love for the two cousins Argemone and Honoria lead him through the famine of 1846 to a Christian socialism.
historical_context: The 1840s, the agricultural depression and Irish famine, the Oxford Movement, and the Christian Socialist experiment of the 1848 revolution.
literary_significance: Yeast is the central English novel of the religious crisis of the 1840s and the first to make a young man's intellectual doubt the subject of a novel; its comic and satirical scenes were admired by Carlyle, and its picture of rural poverty shaped the social-problem novel.

title: Hypatia; or, New Foes with an Old Face
description: Published in 1853 and Kingsley's greatest historical novel: Alexandria in the fifth century, the pagan philosopher Hypatia, and the conflict of Christianity, Judaism and the dying classical world.
plot_or_argument: Philammon, a young Egyptian monk, comes to Alexandria and is caught between the pagan school of Hypatia, the Jewish community of the city and the Christian patriarch Cyril; Hypatia is murdered by the mob, the city is torn apart, and the novel argues for a Christian humanism that can inherit the best of the classical world.
historical_context: The 410s-420s, Alexandria under the Roman Empire, the murder of Hypatia in 415, and the Victorian controversy over the relation of Christianity to classical culture.
literary_significance: Hypatia is the finest English historical novel of late antiquity and a central text in the Victorian debate on the relation of Hellenism and Christianity; its picture of Hypatia shaped the modern legend of the philosopher-martyr.

title: Westward Ho!
description: Published in 1855 and the founding novel of English imperial adventure: the story of Amyas Leigh of Devon in the age of Elizabeth, the Armada and the Spanish Main.
plot_or_argument: Amyas Leigh sails with Drake and Frobisher against the Spaniards, pursues the murderer of his brother across the Atlantic, and is blinded and broken by the vengeance, learning in the end that the destruction of the Spanish empire was the work of God rather than of man.
historical_context: The 1570s-88, the Elizabethan sea-dogs, the Armada of 1588, the Spanish colonies, and the 1850s revival of interest in the Elizabethan age.
literary_significance: Westward Ho! created the English adventure novel of empire: it was the model for Henty, Ballantyne and the whole schoolboy literature of the imperial age, and it made the Elizabethan seaman the central hero of Victorian popular culture.

title: The Water-Babies: A Fairy Tale for a Land-Baby
description: Published in 1863 and the strangest children's classic of the century: the story of Tom, a chimney sweep who drowns and becomes a water-baby, and of his moral and evolutionary education in the rivers and the sea.
plot_or_argument: Tom, brutalised by his master Grimes, is drowned in a Yorkshire river and transformed into a water-baby; he travels down the stream to the sea, is taught by the fairies Mrs Bedonebyasyoudid and Mrs Doasyouwouldbedoneby, searches for Grimes in the Other-end-of-Nowhere, and is finally restored as a man of science.
historical_context: The 1860s, the chimney-sweep scandals and the 1864 Act, Darwin's Origin, the sanitary movement, and the Victorian debate on the education of the poor.
literary_significance: The Water-Babies is the classic English children's book that is also a polemic on sanitation, evolution and education: it is at once a fairy tale, a satire on Victorian science and a plea for the poor child, and it remains one of the most original works of the nineteenth century.

title: Hereward the Wake: 'Last of the English'
description: Published in 1866 and the last of Kingsley's historical novels: the story of the Fenland outlaw who resisted William the Conqueror after 1066.
plot_or_argument: Hereward, outlawed by his own family, returns from exile to find his lands seized, joins the resistance of the Isle of Ely, fights the Normans, and after the fall of Ely escapes and lives as an outlaw, dying in a last fight against Norman knights.
historical_context: The 1066-71 years, the Norman Conquest, the Fenland geography and the legend of Hereward in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the medieval romances.
literary_significance: Hereward the Wake is the founding English novel of the Anglo-Saxon resistance and a key text of Victorian racial and national mythology; its Fenland landscape and its hero made the story of 1066 a central English national legend.

title: Phantastes: A Faerie Romance for Men and Women
description: Published in 1858 and the founding work of modern fantasy: the dream-journey of Anodos through a fairy land, in search of the ideal of beauty and of his own shadow.
plot_or_argument: Anodos, a young man, wakes to find a fairy land in his bedroom and wanders through it, meeting the marble lady, the evil ash-tree, the knight Percivale, and his own shadow; he is destroyed by the shadow and reborn, learning that the ideal he sought was to be found in the ordinary world.
principal_characters: Anodos; the marble lady; Percivale; Cosmo von Wehrstahl; the ash-tree; the shadow
historical_context: The 1850s, German Romanticism, the fairy painting of the Pre-Raphaelites, and the Victorian interest in dreams and the imagination.
literary_significance: Phantastes is the founding text of modern fantasy: it gave the genre its dream-journey structure, its symbolic landscape and its theology of the imagination, and it was the book that converted C. S. Lewis's imagination. It is also a central text of the Victorian revival of the fairy tale for adults.

title: David Elginbrod
description: Published in 1863 and MacDonald's first mature Scottish novel: the education of a young scholar in the household of a Highland peasant, and the first of the great MacDonald studies of Scottish Calvinist piety.
plot_or_argument: Hugh Sutherland, a young tutor, comes to the family of David Elginbrod, a humble and saintly Scottish farmer and beekeeper; Hugh's intellectual pride is tested by David's faith, and after David's death and the loss of his daughter Margaret, Hugh learns to reconcile his learning with a religion of love.
principal_characters: David Elginbrod; Hugh Sutherland; Margaret Elginbrod; Euphra Cameron; Robert Falconer; Lady Emily
historical_context: The 1850s, Scottish Presbyterianism, the Disruption of 1843, and the contrast between the Highland community and the London literary world.
literary_significance: David Elginbrod is the finest Scottish novel of the century after Scott and the most original Victorian fictional portrait of the Calvinist peasant saint; its theology of universal love and its picture of the Scottish household made it a classic of regional fiction.

title: At the Back of the North Wind
description: Published in 1871 and the most beautiful of MacDonald's fairy tales: the story of Diamond, a London cab-horse boy, and his journeys with the North Wind.
plot_or_argument: Diamond meets the North Wind, who appears to him as a beautiful woman, and travels with her through the sky; he is taken to the country at her back, where the river runs through the land, and the novel ends with his early death into that country.
historical_context: The 1870s, the London of the cab trade and the overcrowded poor, and the Victorian allegorical fairy tale after Bunyan.
literary_significance: At the Back of the North Wind is the greatest Victorian children's book about death and the most important influence on C. S. Lewis after Phantastes: its portrait of the dying child and its allegory of the country beyond the wind are among the finest things in English children's literature.

title: The Princess and the Goblin
description: Published in 1872 and the most popular of MacDonald's children's books: the story of Princess Irene, the miner's son Curdie, and the goblins beneath the mountain.
plot_or_argument: Irene, living in a castle under a mountain, meets her mysterious great-great-grandmother in the tower and Curdie, a miner's boy, discovers the goblins' plan to abduct her; together they defeat the goblin court in the underground hall.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian vogue for the fairy tale, and the coal-mining communities of the north.
literary_significance: The Princess and the Goblin is one of the two or three best children's fantasies in English: its great-great-grandmother, the thread, and the underground goblins are permanent images, and the book was a decisive influence on Lewis, Tolkien and the whole modern school of children's fantasy.

title: Lilith: A Romance
description: Published in 1895 and MacDonald's last and darkest fantasy: the dream-journey of Mr Vane into the land of the dead and of the sleeping Lilith.
plot_or_argument: Vane, the last of his family and the owner of an old library, passes through the mirror in the library into a world of skeletons, ravens and dead cities, meets Adam and Eve and the evil princess Lilith, and the novel ends with a vision of universal reconciliation.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian interest in spiritualism, the Swedenborgian and Boehme tradition, and MacDonald's own universalism.
literary_significance: Lilith is the darkest and most theologically daring of the Victorian fantasies and a major influence on the modern adult fantasy: its vision of death, sleep and universal redemption is unique in nineteenth-century literature.

title: Unspoken Sermons
description: Published in three series between 1867 and 1889 and MacDonald's most direct theological writing: sermons on the Fatherhood of God, the will, death and the redemption of all things.
plot_or_argument: The sermons argue that God is a father who will not rest until every child is saved, that hell is a purifying rather than an eternal state, and that obedience to the conscience is the beginning of faith.
historical_context: The 1860s-80s, the Victorian debate on eternal punishment, and the Broad Church movement.
literary_significance: Unspoken Sermons is the most important English statement of universalist theology in the nineteenth century: it influenced Lewis, Chesterton and Barth, and it made MacDonald one of the most original religious thinkers of the Victorian age.

title: The Brownies and Other Tales
description: Published in 1870 and Ewing's best-known collection: the story of a boy who dreams himself into a race of helpful brownies, and other tales of childhood, work and kindness.
plot_or_argument: 'The Brownies' follows Tommy, a lazy boy who is shown the brownies and learns the pleasure of work; the volume also includes 'The Land of Lost Toys', 'Three Christmas Trees' and 'An Idyll of the Wood'.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Victorian children's magazine Aunt Judy's, and the folklore of the household spirit.
literary_significance: The Brownies is a classic of Victorian children's literature and one of the first stories to make work itself a pleasure rather than a duty; its title entered the English language as the name of the junior girl guides.

title: A Flat Iron for a Farthing
description: Published in 1872 and the best of Ewing's longer family stories: the childhood of a boy remembered by himself, and the household of servants, aunts and cousins that made him.
plot_or_argument: The narrator recalls his childhood in a large country house, his father's absence in India, his aunt's rule, the servants who care for him, and the small events — a flat iron, a pony, a Christmas — that shape his character.
historical_context: The 1840s-50s, the English country house and its servants, and the Victorian literature of childhood recollection.
literary_significance: A Flat Iron for a Farthing is one of the finest Victorian children's novels of English family life and a key text in the literature of childhood memory; its picture of the child's world among servants is unmatched in the period.

title: Jan of the Windmill
description: Published in 1876 and Ewing's finest novel: the story of a foundling brought up by a miller, who turns out to have a gift for painting and is torn between the mill and the wider world.
plot_or_argument: Jan, an abandoned child, is raised by the miller Abel Lake and his wife; he shows an early talent for drawing, is taken up by a local artist, is sent to London to study, and returns to the mill to reconcile art with the life that made him.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s, the English windmill economy, the Victorian art world, and the debate on the education of the artist.
literary_significance: Jan of the Windmill is the best English children's novel about the artist's vocation and a key text in the Victorian literature of class and education; its picture of the rural craftsman's world is exact and unsentimental.

title: The Story of a Short Life
description: Published in 1885, the year of her death, and Ewing's most affecting book: the story of a soldier's son, disabled by an accident, who is determined to earn the Victoria Cross.
plot_or_argument: Leonard, the son of a soldier, is crippled in a fall from a horse; he bears his pain with the code of the army, follows the fortunes of the regiment in Egypt, and dies before he can win the cross, having won the love and admiration of the men.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Gordon relief expedition, the Victorian cult of the soldier, and the literature of disabled childhood.
literary_significance: The Story of a Short Life is the classic Victorian children's book about disability and military honour; its portrait of a suffering child and its imperial setting make it a central document of the 1880s and one of the most influential children's books of its decade.

title: Mary's Meadow
description: Published posthumously in 1886 and Ewing's most charming late story: the tale of a child's garden, a family feud over a meadow, and the founding of the Parkinson Flower Show.
plot_or_argument: Mary, a sickly child, is inspired by the seventeenth-century herbalist John Parkinson to plant 'old-fashioned' flowers; she and her brothers make a garden in the meadow, restore the family quarrels, and found a flower show that survives her death.
literary_form: Children's story (published posthumously in Aunt Judy's Magazine)
historical_context: The 1870s-80s, the rural parish, the Victorian flower garden, and the cult of the old-fashioned garden after Ruskin and William Morris.
literary_significance: Mary's Meadow is one of the most beloved Victorian children's stories and a founding text of the English garden literature of childhood; its combination of horticulture, family history and rural community is unique in the period.

title: The Cuckoo Clock
description: Published in 1877 and the most famous of Molesworth's books: the story of Griselda, sent to live with two old aunts, and of the cuckoo in the clock who takes her into the world of the birds.
plot_or_argument: Griselda, lonely and proud, is visited by the cuckoo from the clock in her aunt's hall; he takes her to the court of King Time, where she meets the seasons, the butterflies and the water-sprites, and learns to be less selfish and more patient.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian nursery and the fairy tale, and the child's isolation in the house of elderly relatives.
literary_significance: The Cuckoo Clock is one of the finest Victorian fairy tales and the book that made Molesworth the most popular children's writer of the 1880s; its allegory of time and childhood is a permanent part of the English nursery canon.

title: Carrots: Just a Little Boy
description: Published in 1876 and Molesworth's first great success: the story of a small boy in a large family, his nursery, his sisters and his small adventures.
plot_or_argument: Carrots, the youngest of a family of children, is often overlooked and often naughty; the novel follows his games, his illnesses and his relations with his sisters and the servants, and ends with his growing up into a schoolboy.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian middle-class nursery, and the vogue for realistic family stories after Ewing.
literary_significance: Carrots established Molesworth as the leading children's writer of realistic family fiction and is a key source for the social history of the Victorian nursery; its child's-eye realism was a decisive break with the moral tale of the earlier century.

title: The Tapestry Room: A Child's Romance
description: Published in 1879 and the best of Molesworth's fairy romances: the story of two children who pass through the tapestry in an old French château into the world it depicts.
plot_or_argument: Jeanne and Hugh, staying in an old French house, find that the figures in the tapestry come alive and that the cuckoo clock and the old china provide a way into the past; they meet a mysterious lady and a lost child, and the story ends with the healing of an old family sorrow.
historical_context: The 1870s, the French château, the Victorian taste for the antique, and the fairy tale as a form of historical imagination.
literary_significance: The Tapestry Room is one of the most beautiful Victorian children's fantasies: its idea of entering a tapestry and a past world anticipated the time-slip fantasy of the twentieth century and made Molesworth the equal of MacDonald in the genre.

title: The Carved Lions
description: Published in 1895 and Molesworth's finest late novel: the story of two children sent away to a boarding school, and of the carved lions on the staircase that become their comfort.
plot_or_argument: Geraldine and her brother Lionel are left at a school while their parents are abroad; the girl is lonely and ill-treated, and the carved lions on the stairs become her imaginary protectors until the family returns.
historical_context: The 1890s, the Victorian boarding school, and the literature of the unhappy child.
literary_significance: The Carved Lions is one of the most affecting Victorian children's books about loneliness and the consolations of the imagination; it is a key text in the history of the school story and of children's fantasy.

title: Four Winds Farm
description: Published in 1887 and one of Molesworth's best rural stories: the life of a farm child in the north of England, and the four winds that bring the seasons and the changes of a year.
plot_or_argument: Gratian, a farmer's son, grows up on a moorland farm and learns the work of the seasons; the winds that blow from the four quarters bring visitors, weather and the events that make his childhood.
historical_context: The 1880s, the northern hill farm, and the Victorian children's book of country life.
literary_significance: Four Winds Farm is a fine example of the Victorian rural children's novel and a key text in the literature of the English countryside for children.

title: The Story of the Treasure Seekers
description: Published in 1899 and the book that created the modern children's family story: the Bastable children's attempts to restore the family fortunes, told by one of them who will not say which.
plot_or_argument: Dora, Oswald, Dicky, Alice, Noel and H. O. Bastable, whose mother is dead and whose father is poor, try a series of schemes to make money — digging for treasure, being detectives, publishing a newspaper, selling poetry — each of which fails comically until a real treasure arrives.
principal_characters: Oswald Bastable; Dora Bastable; Dicky Bastable; Alice Bastable; Noel Bastable; H. O. Bastable; Albert-next-door; the Bastables' father
historical_context: The 1890s, the shabby-genteel suburban family, the Victorian cult of the self-help book, and the children's magazine.
literary_significance: The Treasure Seekers invented the modern children's novel of family life: its first-person narrator, its comedy of failure and its unpatronising tone changed the genre, and it was the model for the family story from E. Nesbit to Arthur Ransome.

title: Five Children and It
description: Published in 1902 and the first of the Psammead books: five children on a summer holiday dig up a sand-fairy who grants them one wish a day, and every wish goes wrong.
plot_or_argument: Cyril, Anthea, Robert, Jane and the baby find the Psammead in a gravel pit and wish for beauty, wealth, wings and a castle; each wish is granted literally and ends in disaster, and the children learn to wish for something sensible at last.
historical_context: The 1900s, the English seaside holiday, and the fairy-tale tradition of the three wishes.
literary_significance: Five Children and It is the founding text of the modern comic fantasy for children: its literal-minded magic and its domestic realism created the formula that the twentieth century would develop, and the Psammead is one of the great inventions of children's literature.

title: The Railway Children
description: Published in 1906 and the most popular of Nesbit's books: the story of three children who move to a cottage in the country after their father is arrested, and whose lives are shaped by the railway that runs past their house.
plot_or_argument: Roberta, Peter and Phyllis move with their mother to Three Chimneys, make friends with the stationmaster, the porter and the old gentleman on the train, rescue a boy from a tunnel, prevent an accident by waving a red petticoat, and are finally reunited with their father, who has been cleared of treason.
principal_characters: Roberta (Bobbie); Peter; Phyllis; Mother; Father; Perks the porter; the Old Gentleman; Dr Forrest; Jim
literary_form: Children's novel (serialised in the London Magazine, 1905)
historical_context: The 1900s, the Edwardian railway, the suburban family in reduced circumstances, and the political scandal behind the father's imprisonment.
literary_significance: The Railway Children is one of the best-loved children's novels in English and the classic book of the railway age; its picture of the English countryside, the station and the family in trouble has made it a national institution.
